metadataDescription: An honest orrery: the planets where they really are today, and the clearing of the early solar system as a labelled model, out to the Oort cloud.
canvasLabel: Interactive orrery of the solar system

camera.title: Move the camera
camera.body: Drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom.

views.title: Views
views.body: Jump between scales, out to the Oort cloud.

objects.title: Objects
objects.body: Find a body and open its card.

closeUp.body: Fly in to a body at its true size.

time.title: Time
time.body: Scrub through history, or replay the chapter you are in.

fromEarth.title: From Earth
fromEarth.body: Earth holds still, the Sun circles it and the planets draw their loops: the sky the epicycles explained.

moments.title: Moments
moments.body: Set the clock to an opposition or a conjunction, or the slider to a milestone of deep time.

settings.body: Layers, the camera pad and render quality.

guide.title: Guide
guide.body: Learn how the solar system took shape, step by step.

experiences.title: Viewing modes
experiences.body: Immersive: just the view, no controls. Drift: sit back while the camera flies itself to the music.

viewHints.inner: Mercury to Mars. Jupiter is near the edge.
viewHints.giants: Jupiter to Neptune, and the early disk. The best view of the clearing.
viewHints.kuiper: Neptune's orbit and the Kuiper belt, about {kuiperAu} au.
viewHints.scattered: Bodies Neptune tossed onto long ellipses, hundreds of au out.
viewHints.oort: Guide shells at {oortInnerShellAu} and {oortShellAu} au; the dots thin out as r⁻³·⁵. The distant Oort cloud has not been directly observed; its existence is inferred mainly from the orbits of long-period comets.

moments.vredefort: Vredefort impact; the Moon's youngest sampled lavas

time.protostar: A protostar, not yet the Sun
time.laps: {laps} Galaxy laps since the Sun formed, schematic

solarActivity.description: Hα prominences over the visible-light map: cool plasma held in magnetic dips above polarity-inversion lines, glowing past the limb and dark against the disc. Shapes and timing are authored; a second shows a quarter of an hour, with threads draining and the occasional slow then sudden eruption.

replay.ages: Replay the ages since the clearing

hud.timeSlider: Time. Left is older; the clearing gets extra room on the track.
hud.legend: Switches hide a layer; they do not change the tally.
hud.closeUpNote: True size, turned as it is now.
hud.craftNote: True size, turned to the Sun as it flies.
hud.momentsNote: Found on the JPL orbits; past 2050 the orbits are carried on as they are today.
hud.closeUpPresentOnly: Close-ups show today's surfaces. Return to the present to zoom in.
hud.deepFieldHint: This view today, then on past the nearest stars to the edge of the observable universe.

badges.endMeasured: End orbit measured · start is a model
badges.rewound: Measured end · rewound as a sketch

sun.title: Sun
sun.body: Over {mass} % of the solar system's mass, yet under {spin} % of its angular momentum: nearly all of that rides in the planets' orbits. The clock of this model. Planet positions around it are computed for today's date from the JPL approximate elements, so this is tonight's configuration, seen from above the ecliptic.
sun.caution: Marker sizes are enlarged unless True size is on. The real Sun is {diameters} Earth diameters across and still a speck beside planetary distances.

planets.mercury: Smallest planet. Its path is the most stretched of the eight.
planets.venus: Almost a circle. A circle and an ellipse look the same here.
planets.earth: 1 au is approximately Earth's mean distance from the Sun: {au} km, or {minutes} light-minutes. It is defined as exactly {metres} metres.
planets.mars: A clearly stretched orbit. Still tiny beside Jupiter's.
planets.jupiter: In the model Jupiter starts slightly farther out and ends slightly closer in, as instability studies find. The start is not a measurement. It outweighs all the other planets together more than twice over.
planets.saturn: Starts closer to Jupiter than today, then moves outward in the model. The rings are to scale with the planet. Its mean density is lower than water's.
planets.uranus: An ice giant. In the model it moves outward with Neptune as the disk is stirred. Uranus and Neptune may even have swapped places.
planets.neptune: Ends near {end} at the inner edge of today's Kuiper belt. Its outward move is what scatters the disk in this sketch. Dynamical friction with the disk can then round its orbit again.

cards.planetCautionEllipse: The orbit uses measured elements; during migration, the giant planets’ orbits are adjusted by a teaching model. Playing time speeds up the planet’s orbit.
cards.planetCautionCircle: With Ellipses off, the path is a circle whose radius equals the semi-major axis. The eccentricity shown in the card is unchanged.

ceres.summary: The largest body in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet inside Neptune's orbit: about {share} % of the belt's mass in one world. Dawn orbited it from 2015 to 2018 and found bright salt deposits on a dark, carbon-rich surface.
ceres.caution: The orbit is measured and does not move on the slider: the sketch leaves the belt where it is today.

pluto.summary: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, locked in a 3:2 rhythm with Neptune: Neptune orbits three times while Pluto orbits twice. That is why their paths cross in distance without colliding.
pluto.caution: Today's orbit is from the JPL table. The starting orbit in the sketch, and when it was captured into resonance, are a model of 'moved during Neptune's migration', not a recovered path.

haumea.summary: A dwarf planet that turns once every {spin}, so fast that it is stretched into an ellipsoid twice as long as it is thick. Its surface is crystalline water ice, and a thin ring, not drawn here, was found around it in 2017.
haumea.caution: The body is drawn as a flattened spheroid; the real one is a triaxial ellipsoid. The orbit is measured and does not move on the slider.

makemake.summary: A bright, reddish dwarf planet in the classical Kuiper belt, found in 2005: methane frost over a surface of reddened organics. It has one small, dark moon, found in 2016.
makemake.caution: The orbit is measured and does not move on the slider. Its size comes from a stellar occultation in 2011; its mass is still poorly known.

eris.summary: The most massive dwarf planet, found in 2005: {plutoMasses} times Pluto's mass in a slightly smaller body, on a steeply tilted orbit that swings from Pluto's distance out past twice as far. Its discovery led to the dwarf-planet class in 2006.
eris.caution: The orbit is measured; perihelion comes only in 2257. How Eris got onto so tilted a path is the scattered disk's history, which the slider does not replay.

sedna.summary: A distant dwarf-planet candidate. Its closest point is about {near}, far beyond Neptune, and its far point about {far}. It is detached from the planets and reaches perihelion in 2076.
sedna.caution: The orbit is measured; how Sedna got there is not. A passing star in the Sun's birth cluster is one idea, an unseen distant planet is another. The slider does not invent a path for Sedna.

halley.summary: A famous comet on a long, backward-tilted ellipse: inside Venus's orbit at perihelion, out past Neptune at aphelion. It passed aphelion in December 2023 and returns to perihelion on 28 July 2061.
halley.caution: This is the present orbit, which itself changes a little each return. It is hidden in circle mode: a circle at {a} would park it just inside Uranus's orbit, which is wrong.

asteroids.title: Asteroid belt
asteroids.body: Rocky leftovers between Mars and Jupiter. Jupiter stirred this zone, so collisions broke bodies apart instead of building a planet; many asteroids are fragments of larger bodies, and most of the early mass is gone (not animated here). Spacecraft cross the belt without dodging.
asteroids.caution: Dots are a seeded sample with realistic orbit shapes and the Kirkwood gaps, enlarged, not a catalogue of real asteroids. The two clumps along Jupiter's orbit are its Trojans, most likely captured during the clearing.

disk.title: Early planetesimal disk
disk.when: Only at the old end of the slider
disk.body: A stand-in for the icy leftovers outside the packed giants after the gas disk was gone (about {mass} Earth masses in the Nice model). Neptune's outward move stirs it. It is not a photograph of a particular year.
disk.caution: Studies argue about the disk's mass and outer edge. Round numbers here are for teaching.

kuiper.title: Kuiper belt
kuiper.todayMass: No more than about {value} Earth masses
kuiper.originalMass: Several Earth masses in the classical region; the whole Nice-model disk about {value}
kuiper.body: Icy worlds beyond Neptune, including Pluto. More than {catalogued} trans-Neptunian objects are catalogued; the classical belt fades near {cliff}, the 'Kuiper cliff'. Cold classical dots stay near {cold} the whole time because that population likely formed in place. The stirred dots are the ones Neptune moved, and the dense ring at {plutinos} is the plutinos it captured into the 3:2 resonance.
kuiper.caution: Do not read the two kinds as a census. Today's belt is a thin leftover of a heavier disk.

scattered.title: Scattered disk
scattered.shape: Long ellipses, perihelion still near Neptune
scattered.body: Bodies Neptune scattered onto tall, stretched orbits, still loosely under the planets' influence. Some are slowly lost. Dots bound for the Oort cloud are counted here until their paths are lifted farther out.
scattered.caution: A dot's path is a sketch that ends at a realistic orbit shape. It is not that object's history.

oort.title: Oort cloud
oort.body: A vast swarm of icy bodies proposed in 1950 to explain long-period comets, which arrive from every direction. The giants flung leftovers outward; the Galaxy's tide and passing stars lifted their perihelia out of the planets' reach, so the cloud became a thick shell. It may hold hundreds of billions to trillions of bodies; the dots thin out as r⁻³·⁵, the usual inferred profile.
oort.caution: The distant Oort cloud has not been directly observed. Observed bodies such as Sedna are often classified as inner Oort cloud objects, but the definition of that region varies between studies. The dots in this scene represent a model population; their number does not give the actual number of bodies.

ejected.title: Ejected bodies
ejected.body: Most leftovers never find a quiet home. Jupiter throws many out of the system entirely; the ice giants are better at feeding the Oort cloud because their tosses are gentler. Here a body slides outward on a long ellipse and is then removed. A real ejection is a hyperbola, which is not drawn.
ejected.caution: The fraction is illustrative; published simulations differ. The robust point: most of the original disk is gone.

tracer.title: Small body · {bin}
tracer.cold: Cold-classical stand-in, kept near {range} on purpose.
tracer.ejected: One of the bodies the model removes.
tracer.oort: Bound for the Oort cloud in the model, then lifted off the plane.
tracer.other: Ends in the stirred Kuiper belt or the scattered disk.
tracer.caution: Do not count dots: {count} stand-ins are not {count} real worlds.

observatories.hubble: Above the air that blurs every telescope on the ground, Hubble has looked out since 1990, mostly in visible and ultraviolet light.
observatories.chandra: X-rays never reach the ground. Chandra's long orbit keeps it above Earth's radiation belts for most of each pass.
observatories.webb: Webb looks in the infrared from beyond the Moon, its sunshield keeping the Sun, Earth and Moon on one side. It circles L2 rather than sitting on it.
observatories.elements: Placed by its orbit as tracked on {date}. The orbit holds; the place along it drifts from the real one within days.
observatories.halo: Its loop round L2 is drawn as it looks turning with Earth round the Sun.

linear.title: Distances in the 3D view are linear
linear.body: A step of 10 au is ten times a step of 1 au in every view. Mercury and the Oort cloud cannot share one useful picture: the cloud is tens of thousands of times farther out. Use the views.

size.title: Dot size is not size
size.body: Markers are enlarged so a finger can hit them. True size shrinks planets to real radii and they vanish unless you are very close. That emptiness is the lesson. Colours follow true-colour images; the bright side faces the Sun. Uranus and Neptune's rings are too dark to see; Faint rings shows them in a long exposure, as bright as Saturn's.

today.title: Today is computed
today.body: Planet positions come from the JPL approximate Keplerian elements with their secular rates, computed for the current date. Playing time moves each planet on along today's orbit faster than real time; the orbits themselves stay as measured, since the fitted rates hold only for 1800–2050.

past.title: The past slider is a model
past.body: Nobody has a video of planet positions 4 billion years ago. The old end of the slider is a sketch in the family of the giant-planet instability (the Nice model): giants start closer together with a disk of leftovers outside them; Jupiter and Saturn slowly drift across their 2:1 resonance and the system turns unstable; Neptune's outward move stirs the disk; most bodies are ejected, some stay in the Kuiper belt or the scattered disk, some are handed to the Oort cloud. Newer versions start the giants in a tight chain of resonances that later breaks; the sketch draws the 2005 original, which tied this to the Late Heavy Bombardment {lhbGyr} billion years ago. Recent studies favour an earlier instability, within about 100 million years of the first solids, so a single spike of impacts is no longer the usual picture.

ellipses.title: Ellipses
ellipses.body: On: each path is an ellipse with its real stretch and tilt (or the model's, for bodies being rewound). Off: a circle at the mean distance.

maps.title: Where the Orrery ends
maps.body: Out by the Oort cloud the Galaxy's pull starts to win over the Sun's, and a timeline stops being honest: the Galaxy's own motions over billions of years are not modelled here. Deep Field shows this solar system as it is today and zooms on, past the nearest stars, to the edge of the observable universe.

today.title: Where the planets are today
today.body: Positions computed for today's date from JPL orbital elements. Playing time moves them along these orbits faster.

periods.title: Farther out, slower
periods.body: Earth laps the Sun in a year, Jupiter in {jupiterYears} years, Neptune in {neptuneYears} years. Kepler's third law ties period to distance.
periods.eq: {equation} · P in years, a in au

ellipses.title: Orbits are ellipses
ellipses.body: The Sun sits at one focus. Halley's comet dips inside Venus's orbit and swings out past Neptune's, fastest near the Sun.

scale.title: Mostly empty
scale.body: True size shrinks each planet to its real radius, and at this distance they vanish. The usual markers are enlarged.

birth.title: A cloud falls in
birth.body: A cold core of the cloud falls in under its own weight in about {freeFallKyr} thousand years. Spinning faster as it shrinks, it flattens into a disk, and at the centre a protostar lights, warmed by the fall.

disk.title: Born in a flat disk
disk.body: The planets circle the Sun one way round and almost in one plane. Kant and Laplace took that as the mark of a birth in one spinning cloud of gas and dust. The first solids condensed {sunBirthGyr} billion years ago: the solar system's age.

snowLine.title: The snow line
snowLine.body: Inside about {snowLineAu} au only rock and metal condense; beyond, ice adds mass, so cores grow big enough to grab gas. Where Earth's water came from is debated: from farther out, or already in its rocky building blocks.

assembly.title: The gas goes, the rocks gather
assembly.body: Within about {gasMyr} million years the young Sun's light and wind blow the gas away, and the giants stop growing. Inside, Moon-size embryos collide for tens of millions of years into the rocky planets; a last Mars-size impact on Earth makes the Moon, and near Jupiter the leftovers shatter into the asteroid belt.

clearing.title: The clearing, as a model
clearing.body: The giants start closer together inside a disk of icy leftovers. Jupiter and Saturn drift apart until Saturn's year is twice Jupiter's; that 2:1 resonance shakes the giants loose, and Neptune ploughs out through the disk: most is ejected, some stays in the Kuiper belt or scattered disk, some reaches the Oort cloud.

oort.title: The Oort cloud
oort.body: A proposed shell of icy bodies reaching perhaps {oortShellAu} au. No one has seen it directly; we infer it from long-period comets falling in from it.

technicalDetails.title: Inside the orrery
technicalDetails.summary: Present-day positions from JPL's approximate planetary elements and a labelled teaching model of the early solar system, out to the Oort cloud. The sources below separate measured quantities from sketches.

features.views: Five views from the inner planets to the Oort cloud, each at a linear scale.
features.time: A {timelineGyr}-billion-year timeline with playback, five epochs, and a tally of where the leftover bodies end up.
features.bodies: Planets, Pluto, Sedna, Halley's comet, {tracers} planetesimal stand-ins, GPU swarms for the asteroid belt, the Trojans, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud, and cards that say what is measured.

ephemeris.title: Where the planets are
ephemeris.body: Each planet's a, e, I, L, ϖ and Ω come from the JPL approximate elements for 1800–2050 with linear rates per Julian century. Kepler's equation is solved by Newton's method and the perifocal position is rotated into the J2000 ecliptic frame. Pluto uses its row from the table's earlier edition, since withdrawn by JPL. Sedna and Halley use their osculating elements with the mean anomaly counted from a known perihelion passage. Periods follow Kepler's third law. From Earth, the camera turns about Earth and each trail is a body's position less Earth's over the last years, so the loops of retrograde motion draw as they do in the sky.

formation.title: The Sun's formation
formation.body: A dense core of the natal cloud, {coreDensity} molecules per cubic centimetre, falls in from rest in one free-fall time, about {freeFallKyr} thousand years. The core drawn before the camera shrinks on the cycloid of a uniform sphere, slowly at first, then all at once, spinning up as 1/r² and flattening into a disk. A protostar lights as it lands, {protostarKyr} thousand years before the first solids (the Class 0 phase): an ember through its dust that whitens as it grows, with a first disk a third of the painted one's radius growing out to it. Playback gives the free fall a few seconds and the slider gives the formation a segment of its own. A sketch in time: a real core falls inside out, and a protostar's own light is infrared.

migration.title: Formation and the clearing sketch
migration.body: The first solids condensed {sunBirthGyr} billion years ago (CAI ages); observed disks last about {diskLifetimesMyr} million years, so the giants finish inside a {gasMyr}-million-year gas disk here while the terrestrial planets do most of their growing by {modelStartGyr} billion years ago; the Moon-forming impact, among the last giant collisions, is dated about {moonImpactGyr} billion years ago. Between {modelStartGyr} and {clearDoneGyr} billion years ago the giants interpolate from Nice-model starting orbits ({jupiterStartAu}, {saturnStartAu}, {uranusStartAu} and {neptuneStartAu} au) to their measured ones, and a seeded sample of planetesimals moves from a {diskAu} au disk to the Kuiper belt, the scattered disk, the Oort cloud, or out of the system. The timing is debated: other meteorite studies put the instability soon after the gas cleared. Orbital elements interpolate smoothly; this is not an N-body integration. Before the Sun the solar view shows a schematic molecular cloud with dated galactic milestones as its caption. Inside the gas disk the slider is logarithmic in time since the first solids, so the notes can follow dust (to {planetesimalsKyr} thousand years), planetesimals and Moon-mass embryos (by {embryosMyr} million years). The snow line is drawn at {snowLineAu} au; estimates for the young disk span about {snowLineEstimatesAu} au.

sky.title: The sky behind it
sky.body: Bright stars are the shared J2000 catalogue placed by right ascension and declination and rotated into the planets' ecliptic frame. The Milky Way is sampled from a painted map in galactic coordinates (bulge toward Sagittarius, the Great Rift, the Coalsack): tens of thousands of grains and a soft haze drawn from the same map, so it looks granular like the real band rather than a smooth glow. The whole band turns about the galactic pole once per galactic year as the Sun orbits; before about {thinDiskGyr} billion years ago the thin disk and dust lane give way to a thicker, bluer disk; inside the natal cloud the view dims and reddens. Named stars fade beyond about {namedStarsYears} years, when proper motions have scrambled the constellations.

history.title: Saturn's rings and the Moon's distance
history.body: Saturn's rings are drawn coming in across their dated window, {ringsMyr} million years ago: nothing in the model forms them. The Moon is drawn from the narrated impact on, starting just outside the fluid Roche limit, about {moonFormedKm} km, and receding through the tidal records to today's {moonKm} km: about {moodiesShare} % of today's distance {moodiesGyr} billion years ago from the Moodies tidal bundles, {joffreKm} km {joffreGyr} billion years ago from the Joffre banded iron, {xiamalingKm} km {xiamalingGyr} billion years ago from the Xiamaling Formation, {elatinaKm} km {elatinaMyr} million years ago from the Elatina rhythmites. Between records the distance follows the constant-torque law, a^(13/2) linear in time, a sketch: the real rate swung with the oceans' tidal resonances. The orbit is drawn at the system's magnified scale, so the scene shows the distance against today's and True size keeps it real; the Moon's card prints it at the selected time.

youngSun.title: The faint young Sun
youngSun.body: On the main sequence the Sun brightens as its core turns hydrogen to helium. Gough's interpolation of standard solar models gives its output by age: about {youngSunPercent} % of today's as the sketch starts, within a few per cent of the models after its first few hundred million years. The glow follows the law; the contracting Sun before the sketch is not modelled, and the band is not drawn there. The habitable zone is drawn at its conservative edges today, {zoneInnerAu} to {zoneOuterAu} au (moist to maximum greenhouse, clouds left out), and moved with the square root of the output, where the same sunlight falls; the young Sun's redder light would move both edges slightly back out. The Sun's card reads both at the selected time.

events.title: Moments on the clock
events.body: Each moment in the Objects panel is found on the same orbits the scene draws, not typed in: a scan from today brackets the next (or last) date where its condition crosses zero, a bisection narrows the bracket to the hour. A planet is at opposition when its heliocentric longitude meets Earth's; two planets are in conjunction when their longitudes seen from Earth meet; perihelion is where the distance's rate of change turns upward; a transit is an inferior conjunction with Mercury inside the Sun's disc. The JPL elements are fitted for 1800–2050; a later date carries them on as they are, and the panel says so. Picking a moment sets the clock to its date; playing time runs on from there, and Today brings it back.

swarms.title: Belts and clouds on the GPU
swarms.body: The asteroid belt, Jupiter's Trojans, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud are point swarms whose vertex shader solves Kepler's equation each frame, so thousands of bodies orbit at the same speed-up as the planets in one draw call each. The belt has Kirkwood gaps; the Trojans librate about L4 and L5 and appear during the clearing; the Kuiper belt holds cold classicals formed in place, hot classicals, plutinos at {plutinosAu} au and twotinos at {twotinosAu} au swept into resonance by Neptune, and nothing beyond the cliff; the Oort cloud thins as r⁻³·⁵ from an inner, flatter cloud to an isotropic shell at {oortShellAu} au.

globes.title: Globes and rings
globes.body: Radii, flattening and poles are IAU values and spin rates IAU or newer measurements (Venus, Saturn, Uranus), so every globe has its real shape and turns to today's angle: Uranus lies on its side, Venus spins backwards. Surfaces are measured maps: Hubble's 2025 maps of the giants, Blue Marble Earth, Viking Mars, MESSENGER Mercury and New Horizons Pluto, with mean colour and brightness set by true-colour data and albedo. The Sun uses a representative SDO/HMI photosphere mosaic from 1–22 May 2024, reprojected across one rotation with quiet polar fill; its sunspots are not live or tied to the timeline date. Rings use measured radii and optical depths, lit from the front or seen against the light, with the planet's shadow across them. Jupiter's are too faint to show. The Moon uses LRO/LROC imagery; Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Triton use Voyager/Galileo mosaics, Charon uses New Horizons, Phobos and Deimos use Viking-based mosaics, and Saturn's mid-size moons use Cassini mosaics. Some moon maps are monochrome or use muted multispectral colour, not calibrated natural colour. Unobserved moon terrain uses plain fill; source polar interpolation is documented in the credits. Venus and Titan retain illustrative clouds and haze; Sedna, Halley and Uranus's moons retain illustrative surfaces.

observatories.title: Observatories near Earth
observatories.body: Hubble and Chandra move on their latest CelesTrak element sets: Kepler's ellipse about Earth, its size from the mean motion and its plane and perigee turned by Earth's equatorial bulge (J2). Their drag term moves the place on as the orbit sinks. That keeps each orbit right for months; the place along it drifts within days to weeks, as drag changes and the Moon's and Sun's pulls are left out. Webb flies its JPL Horizons trajectory, as flown and then as predicted, kept in the frame that turns with Earth round the Sun, where its loop round L2 holds still, and drawn about the Earth the scene shows. L2 itself follows from the Sun's, Earth's and the Moon's masses. They show only near Earth and only today, at their true distances, and fly in at their true size: NASA's models, scaled by published widths, their solar arrays (Webb: its sunshield) turned to the Sun.

rendering.title: Rendering budget
rendering.body: One instanced mesh draws all planetesimals, orbit lines are rewritten only when their elements change, and frames are rendered only while something moves or a setting changed. Coarse-pointer or low-memory devices cap the pixel ratio and frame rate. Globes switch to a finer mesh only when they are large on screen.

notes.merger: About {mergerGyr} billion years ago the Milky Way swallows the Gaia-Enceladus galaxy, stirring and thickening the thick disk that is already forming. The atoms that will make the Sun are still interstellar gas.
notes.thinDisk: By about {thinDiskGyr} billion years ago the thin disk is forming stars and the Galaxy's bar is in place. Earlier generations of stars are forging the heavy elements the Sun will inherit.
notes.ingredients: Interstellar gas, enriched by earlier generations of stars. The cloud that will become the Sun has not yet collapsed.
notes.core: A cold, dense core turns slowly inside the cloud: about {coreDensity} molecules per cubic centimetre. Short-lived aluminium-26 in meteorites hints at a massive star nearby.
notes.collapse: The core falls in under its own weight, taking about {freeFallKyr} thousand years at this density: slowly at first, then all at once. As it shrinks it spins faster and flattens into a disk.
notes.protostar: A protostar glows at the centre, heated by the infalling gas and hidden in dust, feeding from the disk around it. The first solids condense about {protostarKyr} thousand years later.
notes.dust: The first solids condense {sunBirthGyr} billion years ago: the timeline's zero. Dust grains stick when they touch gently and grow into pebbles a millimetre to a centimetre across.
notes.planetesimals: In models the pebbles gather within about {planetesimalsKyr} thousand years into planetesimals kilometres across; farther out this takes millions of years. Arrokoth is one that survived.
notes.gasDisk: Models grow Moon-mass embryos within about {embryosMyr} million years. Beyond the snow line, ice-rich cores grow fast enough to capture gas and become the giant planets.
notes.jupiterCore: Meteorites fall into two isotopic families that stayed apart from about {jupiterCoreMyr} million years after the first solids: Jupiter's core had grown massive enough to wall the outer disk off from the inner.
notes.marsHalf: Hafnium–tungsten clocks in Martian meteorites show Mars half-grown about {marsHalfMyr} million years after the first solids: a planetary embryo that stopped growing.
notes.accretion: The young Sun's light and wind blow the gas away. Inside, many Moon-sized embryos remain, and Jupiter's pull sets their orbits crossing.
notes.belt: Far from Jupiter, slow collisions merge the embryos into rocky planets. Near Jupiter the collisions are fast and shatter them: the asteroid belt.
notes.moon: In the leading model a Mars-sized body strikes Earth and the Moon forms from the debris. Dates span about {moonImpactGyr} billion years ago; the younger ones may record later remelting. The Moon gathers just outside the Roche limit, and the tides push it outward: its drawn orbit grows through the dated records.
notes.disk: The sketch's starting state: the giants packed close, a heavy disk of icy bodies beyond them. The starting orbits are a teaching choice.
notes.clearing: The clearing, as a model: Jupiter and Saturn cross a resonance, the giants scatter one another, and Neptune scatters the disk.
notes.earthCrust: Zircons from Jack Hills show Earth had a crust {earthCrustGyr} billion years ago, and one cool enough for liquid water soon after: the first oceans.
notes.bombardment: Many Apollo impact melts date to about {lhbGyr} billion years ago: the classic Late Heavy Bombardment. Much of that debris may come from a single basin, Imbrium, so whether it was a spike or a long decline is still debated.
notes.marsDynamo: Mars's dynamo is still magnetising lavas {marsDynamoGyr} billion years ago. Later its global field fails, and the solar wind strips the atmosphere away.
notes.marsDry: Around {marsDryGyr} billion years ago Mars's Hesperian period ends: the rivers and lakes are mostly gone, and the cold desert begins.
notes.vredefort: {vredefortGyr} billion years ago an asteroid carves Vredefort, the largest confirmed impact structure on Earth. On the Moon, the youngest lavas yet sampled flow {moonLavaGyr} billion years ago, dated by Chang'e 5's basalts; its glass beads record eruptions as late as about {moonGlassMyr} million years ago.
notes.saturnRings: Saturn's rings may be young: Cassini's count of infalling dust gives them {ringsMyr} million years, though little of that dust may stick, so they could be far older. Nothing in the model forms them; the drawn rings arrive across that window.
notes.chicxulub: {chicxulubMyr} million years ago an asteroid strikes Chicxulub, in Yucatán, and the Cretaceous ends.
notes.today: Measured orbits: the planets stand where they are on the clock's date.
